Title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv’s strike on Russian ships in Benghazi condemned by Libya’s UN-backed government

- **Libya’s foreign ministry condemned an attack on two Russian ships near the eastern city of Benghazi claimed by Ukraine, demanding an explanation from Kyiv**. The attacks caused the Russian corvette Merkury to explode and sink at the port of Benghazi, while a dry cargo vessel was also hit. Ukraine said Russia was using it to transport weapons. The Tripoli-based foreign ministry of Libya’s UN-recognised government condemned the “conduct of any foreign military operations within Libyan territory or territorial waters”.
- **Ukraine confirmed it deployed naval drones in the strikes on the two Russian vessels off Libya,** Peter Beaumont reports. Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”. The Guardian identified more than 460,000 deaths linked to the war between the start of the invasion in February 2022 and September 2026. War became the leading cause of death in Russian men under 65 last year. The real toll is likely to be higher. The deaths of missing soldiers are often registered months or years later, when bodies are recovered or courts declare men dead, and the records thin out sharply in 2026, even though the fighting has remained exceptionally deadly.

The deaths of a further 885 soldiers in or near Ukraine were recorded as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”, a classification that experts say can conceal suicides and that was used in several cases independently identified by the Guardian as suicides. Title: Ukraine war briefing: Stop using teargas on battlefield, dozens of countries tell Russia
URL: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/26/ukraine-war-briefing-stop-using-tear-gas-on-battlefield-dozens-of-countries-tell-russia

<article>
- **Officials from 34 countries and the EU have called on Russia to stop using riot-control gas on the battlefield**, after the global chemical weapons watchdog confirmed that Ukraine had found traces of teargas in a trench Kyiv said was hit with a Russian grenade. The joint statement was issued on Wednesday in response to a Ukrainian report circulated to 193 countries as the Organisation ‌for the Prohibition of Chemical ‌Weapons (OPCW) gathered in The Hague this week. Ukraine said it had documented more than 14,000 ‌cases of munitions filled with riot-control agents and toxic chemicals used by Russia on the frontline since 2022. The OPCW said laboratories approved by the watchdog had “confirmed the presence of a riot-control agent (CS)” in samples collected at the trench.
- **Riot-control agents such as CS, a form of teargas, are banned in warfare**. “We call for the immediate cessation of the use of any toxic chemicals and of riot control agents as a method of warfare in Ukraine,” non-proliferation directors from Britain, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand and the EU, among others, said in a statement. News reports midyear said western intelligence had found that Russian forces were using riot-control agents to drive Ukrainian troops out of trenches and into the open so they could fire on them. Russia has denied using illegal munitions, and has accused Ukraine of doing so.
- **At least five people were killed and three injured in a drone attack ‌on ‌a car ‌park in Vesioloye in the Russian-occupied part of ‌Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region**, Russian-installed governor Yevgeny Balitsky said on Thursday. In Russia, debris from drones shot down over the Tuymazinsky district in the Bashkortostan region fell in an industrial zone and caused a fire, the head of the district ‌said.
- **Russian forces carried out a huge overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting military-industrial facilities in Kyiv**, the ‌Interfax ‌news agency quoted the defence ministry as saying on Thursday. ****Late on Wednesday, Russian forces attacked the Ukrainian capital with ballistic missiles, striking a shopping centre and two other buildings, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Three people were wounded, with one in a serious condition, he said, warning residents to ‌remain in shelters.
- **Ukrainian forces struck a major airbase in Russia, damaging five planes** used to launch missiles and bombs at Ukraine, the Ukrainian general staff said. Russia did not immediately comment on Wednesday’s claim, which said the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region had been hit in Kyiv’s latest long-range attack. Three MiG-31 jets and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were knocked out of operation “for some time”, the general ‌staff said.
- **German chancellor Friedrich Merz accused Russia of “escalating” threats to European security** as he defended his government’s plans to bolster defence spending and maintain financial aid to Ukraine. Opposition parties, including on the far right and hard left, have called for an end to aid to Kyiv. “It cannot be said often enough, against the far right as much as the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine,” Merz told the Bundestag. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea; Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is by now also escalating ‌massively here in our own ‌country.”
- **US envoy Jared Kushner has warned against a downward spiral in the Ukraine conflict, which he called “a proxy war** where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia”. He told a German podcast that “it won’t take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively”. Kushner also appeared to accuse the Europeans of hypocrisy for continuing to buy Russian energy while backing Ukraine.
- **Poland will create a no-fly zone near the Ukrainian border**, a deputy defence minister has announced, after several incursions into its airspace, which it blamed on Russia. The no-fly zone is intended to allow Polish forces to quickly identify any Russian military aircraft and shoot them down if necessary.

- **Nine more Ukrainian children have been reunited with their families amid the war in Ukraine**, bringing the total to 43, under an initiative led by US first lady Melania Trump, the White House and Russia said on Wednesday. There was no immediate comment from Ukrainian authorities.

Title: Armenia plans full withdrawal of Russian border guards in coming years, prime minister says
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/armenia-plans-full-withdrawal-of-russian-border-guards-in-coming-years-prime-minister-says

<article>
Armenia plans to gradually replace Russian border guards with its own forces, ending Russia's decades-long role in guarding the country's borders, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said on Nov. 26.

Speaking at a press briefing following a government meeting, Pashinyan said Armenia intends to assume full responsibility for protecting its borders in the coming years.

"We are grateful to the Russian border guards for having stood at our borders all these years. But I believe the time has come for us to fully assume responsibility for protecting our borders in the coming years," Pashinyan said.

Russian border guards, operating under Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), have helped protect Armenia's borders with Turkey and Iran under a bilateral agreement signed in 1992.

Their presence has gradually diminished as Yerevan has moved to take greater control of its border security.

Russian personnel withdrew from Yerevan's Zvartnots International Airport in August 2024. Armenian border guards also assumed sole responsibility for the Agarak crossing on the Iranian border in January 2025 and the Margara crossing on the Turkish border in February 2025.

Russian and Armenian border guards have continued to jointly patrol other sections of the borders with Turkey and Iran.

Pashinyan did not provide a specific timeline for completing the withdrawal.

The announcement comes amid deteriorating relations between Armenia and Russia, traditionally a key security partner. Yerevan froze its participation in the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) in February 2024, accusing the alliance of failing to fulfill its security obligations during confrontations with Azerbaijan.
</article>

Title: Starshield restrictions still hampering Ukraine's drone defenses, Zelensky tells BBC
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/starshield-restrictions-still-hampering-ukraines-drone-defenses-zelensky-tells-bbc

<article>
Restrictions on the U.S.-provided Starshield satellite communications system continue to undermine Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the BBC published on Nov. 26.

Zelensky confirmed that restrictions on Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, remained in place in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine, affecting Ukrainian drone operations.

Ukrainian drone operators told the BBC that their interceptor drones could no longer keep up with Russian Shahed-type drones, allowing some to penetrate deeper into Ukrainian territory.

Asked who was responsible for the restrictions, Zelensky said the situation remained unclear.

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," he said. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

The restrictions have been a point of contention between Kyiv and Washington in recent weeks. Earlier in November, Zelensky called on the United States and Elon Musk's SpaceX to remove speed limits on Starshield terminals, warning that they were undermining Ukraine's defenses against Russian drones.

Zelensky also expressed frustration over delays in American deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors, saying Ukraine continued to face a severe shortage of missiles capable of stopping Russian ballistic attacks.

The president criticized Washington for prioritizing the Middle East over Ukraine, describing the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors as "very, very big."

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

The president said Ukraine's military is now intercepting about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, although he acknowledged the country faces significant challenges in protecting its skies.

The restrictions and shortages come as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter, leaving repair crews struggling to restore electricity and heating across several regions.

Recent Russian strikes have also targeted bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv, while jet-powered drones continue to threaten the capital and other major Ukrainian cities.

Zelensky acknowledged that Ukraine was facing a difficult winter but pledged to defend Kyiv amid mounting Russian attacks.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country," Zelensky said.
</article>

U.S. President Donald Trump departed from a published joint statement with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Nov. 26, adding Ukraine to a warning against expanding the war that was originally directed solely at Russia.

Trump and Rutte met at the U.S. president's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Nov. 25, with Russia's war against Ukraine and the conflict in Iran among the primary topics of discussion.

The White House did not respond to Politico's request for comment.

Trump also expressed optimism about the possibility of reaching a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.

The revised wording comes as European leaders grapple with the risk of the war spreading beyond Ukraine's borders.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul separately warned against the geographical expansion of the war on Nov. 26, while reaffirming their countries' support for Ukraine.

President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Nov. 23 that Ukrainian forces had sunk the Russian corvette Merkury in the Mediterranean Sea off the coast of Benghazi, Libya.

NATO foreign ministers are scheduled to meet in Brussels on Dec. 2.

Title: Ukrainian forces strike ballistic missile fuel production plant in Russia's Tula Oblast, military confirms
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/explosions-reported-at-power-plant-synthetic-rubber-factory-in-russias-tula-oblast-following-drone-attack

<article>
*Editor's note: The story was updated with a report from Ukraine's General Staff.*

Ukraine targeted a Russian facility involved in producing solid rocket fuel, striking the Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in Tula Oblast overnight on Nov. 27, the General Staff confirmed.

Videos purportedly showing the attack began circulating on social media overnight. Russian independent outlet Astra identified an explosion at the Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant after analyzing footage shared online.

The outlet also reported an explosion at the Efremov thermal power plant, which supplies heat and electricity to the city and local industrial facilities, including the rubber plant. Local residents reported disruptions to their heating supply following the explosions.

The operation was carried out by Ukrainian forces in cooperation with the Black Spark ("Chornaya Iskra" in Russian) resistance movement operating in Russia, the General Staff said.

Synthetic rubber is a key component of solid rocket fuel, and the plant manufactures fuel used in Iskander ballistic missiles, according to the General Staff.

"Without it, the Iskander is just a piece of metal sitting in storage. These are the very missiles Russia's army uses to strike Ukrainian cities, energy infrastructure, and civilian targets," the General Staff said.

The full extent of the damage is still being assessed, the General Staff added.

In a statement on Nov. 27, the General Staff also confirmed a strike on the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery in Russia's Rostov Oblast, which has an annual processing capacity of up to 7.5 million metric tons of oil. The strike destroyed 20 horizontal storage tanks and damaged another 21 horizontal tanks, 11 vertical tanks, and a section of pipeline.

Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyayev said on Telegram that Russian air defenses had downed four Ukrainian drones over the region, adding that the threat of further drone attacks remained.

"There were no casualties. According to preliminary information, no damage to infrastructure has been recorded," Milyayev said.

The governor said falling drone debris had damaged windows at three private residences in the Efremov district but made no mention of explosions at either industrial facility.

The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports.

The Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant has been targeted in previous Ukrainian attacks, including on Dec. 24, 2025, and Sept. 25, 2026.

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted facilities within Russia linked to its military-industrial complex in an effort to undermine Moscow's ability to sustain its war.
</article>

Title: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4gnm3m9deno

<article>
- Published

**European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.**

Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.

Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.

Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget.

"I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters.

"The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council.

EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending.

France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".

Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency.

Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected."

Title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,648,161 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/general-staff-russia-has-lost-1-648-161-troops-in-ukraine-since-feb-24-2022

<article>
Russia has lost 1,648,161 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Nov. 26.

The number includes 2,262 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.

According to the **report**, Russia has also lost 12,514 tanks, 26,003 armored combat vehicles, 180,752 vehicles and fuel tanks, 52,858 artillery systems, 2,306 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,772 air defense systems, 456 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,243 unmanned ground vehicles, 36 ships and boats, and two submarines.

Russia has lost 432,519 troops so far in 2026, marking its highest annual losses since the start of the full-scale invasion and surpassing the previous record of 430,790 set in 2024, Ukraine's General Staff **reported** on Nov. 24.

Russian battlefield losses have been especially heavy in recent months. October 2026 was the **deadliest month** for Russian troops since the start of the full-scale invasion, with 54,400 personnel killed, wounded, or missing, according to Ukraine's General Staff.

The losses continued to mount in November, with Russia losing 2,980 troops in a single day on Nov. 8 — the **highest daily figure** reported since February 2022, the General Staff **said** on Nov. 9.

Russian independent media outlet Mediazona said on Nov. 23 that around 700,000 **Russian soldiers** had been killed in the war, citing its analysis of recently leaked data from Rosstat, Russia's state statistics agency.

A screenshot of the website of Myrotvorets, a Ukrainian site founded in 2014 that publishes a database of people it says support Russia's aggression against Ukraine. (Myrotvorets)

Over the past month, a Ukrainian website's decision to expose Italian lawmakers for their pro-Russian statements has sparked an international scandal.

But the controversy has also highlighted a deeper problem with the website itself.

Founded in 2014 to identify people supporting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, the Myrotvorets website has evolved into a controversial database with no clearly defined allegiance or transparent methodology.

Alongside genuine Russian collaborators, propagandists, and war criminals, the site has listed pro-Ukrainian journalists, politicians critical of the authorities, and public figures who have consistently opposed Russia’s aggression.

Some of them later received threats and viewed the website as a blacklist designed to intimidate them.

Myrotvorets had previously been accused of having ties to the Ukrainian authorities under ex-President Petro Poroshenko. The administration of his successor, Volodymyr Zelensky, who has himself faced criticism from the site, denies any such links.

Mykyta Poturayev, a lawmaker from Zelensky's Servant of the People party, praised Myrotvorets for identifying genuine pro-Russian figures and war criminals. However, he stressed that "unfortunately Myrotvorets is not a verified source."

"There is no way to independently verify its findings or the information in its database based on its methodology," he said.

"If you want to avoid controversy and have your work taken seriously, you should have a clear procedure for determining who gets added to your database."

Political analyst Volodymyr Fesenko went further, arguing that the controversies surrounding the site meant Myrotvorets "has done more harm than good to Ukraine's interests, particularly its international interests."

Myrotvorets declined to comment. The Kyiv Independent has also requested comment from the President's Office and will publish its response once received.

## `Italian scandal`

In 2017, Myrotvorets added Mateo Salvini, who is now an Italian deputy prime minister from the right-wing Lega party, to its list, due to his support for Russia’s illegal annexation of Ukraine's Crimea and his visit to the occupied peninsula in 2014.

On Nov. 16, 2026, Myrotvorets also listed seven members of the European Parliament from the Italian populist party Five Star Movement.

The lawmakers have made pro-Russian statements and opposed Italian aid to Ukraine.

The decision prompted a backlash from Italy, with Salvini calling for removing Italian citizens from Myrotvorets' database and banning the site. Italian Prime Minister Georgia Meloni has also protested against the move.

Ukraine's Foreign Ministry has argued that Myrotvorets has no links to the Ukrainian authorities.

Salvini's name was removed from the site amid the recent scandal, but the European MPs' names remained.

"These publications can harm us because they spark controversies and unfortunately play into the hands of political forces that may oppose support for Ukraine," Fesenko said. "The Interior Ministry, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), intelligence agencies and the Border Guard Service have long used information from the Myrotvorets site to gather intelligence, launch criminal investigations and obtain court orders to detain and arrest separatists and terrorists," Herashchenko wrote in 2014.

Avakov was interior minister until 2021.

Myrotvorets has denied being run by Tuka or Herashchenko or being linked to Poroshenko, Avakov or the Ukrainian authorities in general.

Currently, Myrotvorets is headed by Roman Zaitsev, who says he is a former Security Service (SBU) employee. Zaitsev denied having links to or working with the government.

Specifically, journalists from Reuters, BBC, CNN, Agence France-Presse, Associated Press and other international outlets, as well as Roman Tsymbaliuk, a Ukrainian journalist critical of the Kremlin, were affected.

The Committee to Protect Journalists condemned the publication, interpreting it as an assault on free speech.

At the time, Myrotvorets was also accused of being used as a political tool by Poroshenko and Avakov.

Ex-Georgian President Mikhail Saakashvili's name was added to Myrotvorets' database in 2017 for allegedly illegally crossing the Ukrainian border and preparing a "coup d'etat" against the Ukrainian government.

Saakashvili, a pro-Western politician and one of Putin's most prominent foes, moved to Ukraine in 2015 but later fell out with then President Poroshenko. He also accused Poroshenko and Avakov of corruption.

Saakashvili was stripped of his Ukrainian citizenship, prosecuted and then deported by the Ukrainian authorities in 2018 in what he believes to be an unlawful political vendetta.

Title: Why Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary, and Slovakia are complicating the latest EU push for a Ukraine loan
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/why-bulgaria-czechia-hungary-and-slovakia-are-complicating-the-latest-eu-push-for-a-ukraine-loan

<article>
**BRUSSELS, Belgium —** EU leaders failed to significantly advance key talks on financial support for Ukraine and the bloc's next multi-year budget at Nov. 26-27 summit in Brussels, with four EU countries preventing agreement on a key loan for Kyiv.

For Ukraine, leaders both had to grapple with how to provide long-term financial support in the 2028-2034 budget, as well as approve a 45 billion euro ($49 billion) loan proposed by the European Commission, which would help fill a projected 70 billion euro hole in Kyiv's 2027 budget.

"24 member states supported the proposal... we will revert to this question in December," said European Council President Antonio Costa, at a press conference in the early hours of Nov. 27.

But the loan itself functions as a single borrowing action from the EU on the markets. It is not treated as two distinct debts to repay, one for defense spending and one not.

Likewise, there is no clarity on how Bulgaria could only contribute in areas where there is a Bulgarian-speaking minority in Ukraine in practice.

If approved, the loan would be provided to Ukraine's national government, and spent on national spending priorities defined by Kyiv.

Hungary, Czechia, and Slovakia, the remaining hold-outs, hope to repeat the opt-out they secured on a previous EU loan of 90 billion euros ($99 billion), approved for Kyiv in April.

But a long list of leaders made clear ahead of the leaders' summit that they will not support countries opting out of support for Ukraine.

And at the end of the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz repeated his position that "support for Ukraine has to be borne by the European Union, and all of them (member states)."

But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis called Merz's attempts to force that position through "completely absurd," in remarks to journalists made ahead of the EU leaders' summit.

But while Bulgaria agreed to support the loan, with Sofia supporting only the civilian component, Magyar expressed uncertainty about how that split could work and be upheld.

Fico told Slovakia's European Affairs committee on Nov. 25, the day before the summit, that he also thinks "every country should have the right to express its own form of solidarity with Ukraine."

He called the idea of countries being able to contribute only to the civilian part of the loan "a kind of trick on the part of the Commission."

"I am pleased that there is wide support for our proposal ... now it is in the Council's hand to finalize the work and we will of course be supportive," was all that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on the topic at a post-summit press conference.

Fico also cast doubts on the wider principle of providing financial support to Ukraine.

He said he was not "entirely convinced that giving money to Ukraine is the right thing to do," because of "the massive corruption scandals that regularly shake Ukraine, as well as shocking estimates of how much of this money is actually stolen."

Fico provided no numbers to support his claim.

For the defense spending portion of the loans to Ukraine — which covers two-thirds of the total — Kyiv has to submit shopping lists to the EU before making purchases and provide receipts post-purchase to receive funds.

Fico added that for him, the 45 billion loan is "not a loan in the real sense of the word. It is a pure grant, because the European Commission's documents explicitly state that the loan will be repaid by Ukraine only after Russia pays war reparations to Ukraine."

"We all know very well that nothing of the sort will happen," Fico added.

On this last point, Fico could have a point, though the Commission proposals also mention that in the scenario where Russia does not agree to pay reparations, the more than 200 billion euros in Russian immobilized assets held in the bloc "may" be used.

If those assets are not used in that scenario, the EU would be liable for paying the entire amount.

And for Babis, he expressed fear that the amounts required to support Ukraine in the long run could spiral.

"I want to ask what the goal is. Every year we will pay Ukraine 135 billion euros. Until when? How many years? 10, 20, 30? What kind of strategy is this?" Babis asked, in remarks to journalists made ahead of the EU leaders' summit.

"Russia's unconventional war on Europe has so far failed in its strategic purpose," the report , said, noting that military aid to Ukraine continues and European defense spending rose by 12.6% in 2025.

Despite continued European support for Ukraine and increased defense spending, the report warns that "a mass-casualty incident is possible as the space for miscalculation narrows."

European countries have strengthened their defenses through new security strategies, the expulsion of Russian intelligence officers, arrests of suspected operatives and the closure of Russian consulates. German authorities accuse him of helping to place explosives on the pipelines as part of a covert operation conducted from a rented sailing yacht that departed from the port of Rostock.

The appeals court found the lower court's decision premature and asked it to seek further clarification from German authorities on the two European arrest warrants, the charges, and the scope of the criminal proceedings.

"(Zhuravliov's) extradition to Germany remains an open question," the Ukrainian law firm said on Facebook.

Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.

The Polish court argued that the Nord Stream sabotage could be considered a justifiable act in the context of Ukraine's defense against Russia.

German investigators previously linked the sabotage to a pro-Ukraine group, allegedly led by another Ukrainian national, Serhii Kuznietsov, who is already in German custody after being detained in Italy in August 2025.

Kyiv has denied any involvement in the explosions.

The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics. Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

Title: Russia developing new satellite communications system for military use, HUR says
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/russia-developing-new-satellite-communications-system-for-military-use-hur-says

<article>
Russia is expanding its existing Rassvet military satellite network while developing a second system, called Innosat, Ukraine's military intelligence deputy chief, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, said in an interview with The Times published on Nov. 25.

The statement comes as Russia continues to expand its military satellite network after SpaceX introduced mandatory Starlink registration for users in Ukraine, significantly disrupting Russian operations.

Unlike other forms of communication, satellite-based systems provide a more resilient, harder-to-jam internet connection, allowing troops to be commanded and coordinated, and drones to be operated in real time on the battlefield.

Innosat is a new low-Earth-orbit satellite project developed by St. Petersburg-based Geoscan as part of Russia's 10-year plan to deploy 240 satellites by 2036, according to Skibitskyi.

Meanwhile, Russia is already using Rassvet, a low-Earth-orbit satellite communications network developed by Russian company Bureau 1440, as an alternative to Starlink and plans to expand its constellation to 924 satellites by 2035, the official said.

Of the 32 Rassvet satellites launched this year, 30 are currently operational, but their coverage over Ukraine remains intermittent, lasting no more than 40 minutes at a time. Technical problems have also led Russia to delay the launch of another 16 satellites.

HUR estimated that Russia's Rassvet and InnoSat networks will support around 22,000 terminals combined, compared with more than 10 million users on Starlink.

Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) has also identified 49 Russian companies involved in developing the network and plans to target their production capabilities through "all possible means," ranging from long-range strikes to sabotage, Skibitsky said.

Skibitskyi also warned that Russia's expanding network of low-orbit satellites could have security implications far beyond Ukraine.

"Russia could equip different weapons with receivers for this network and use them all over the world. It would allow Moscow to operate naval drones or unmanned aircraft in regions far beyond the Black Sea — in Europe, Africa, the Middle East or the Far East," the general told The Times.
</article>
